x_to_y: This edge encodes that changes in \(x\) cause changes in \(y\), i.e., shifting \(x\) (holding other relevant factors fixed) would move the expected level of \(y\). The main threats to interpreting an estimated \(x \rightarrow y\) effect causally are confounding (omitted variables that affect both \(x\) and \(y\)), reverse causality if \(y\) also influences \(x\), and measurement error in \(x\) that can attenuate or distort the estimated effect. Next, the researcher should articulate and test a credible identification strategy (e.g., randomized variation, quasi-experimental instrument, or panel with fixed effects and plausible timing), and check balance/placebo tests or pre-trends to probe whether variation in \(x\) is as-good-as-random with respect to determinants of \(y\).
